summary: Asteroid Watch preserves space data for future research through two working components. A public SPHEREx viewer presents real infrared cutouts of interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS from August and December 2025, with observation dates, sky coordinates, metadata, and original FITS downloads. A demonstration dashboard also shows an archived asteroid record and the human-review process. Separately, a NASA NeoWs pipeline archives asteroid catalogue snapshots and reviewed AI summaries in Supabase, while an ESP32, Uno R3, and LCD display saved collection status. Preserving source inputs, dates, model versions, and review decisions makes the historical record available for later inspection. This is a limited first image-viewing case study for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. The images and cloud archive currently operate separately; the public dashboard is not a live database connection. Registered comparisons and linking image evidence to the database are future work. The prototype does not claim new-object discovery, image-based AI detection, impact prediction, or a NASA partnership.
details:
Asteroid Watch preserves astronomical evidence for future inspection.

The SPHEREx viewer shows two real infrared cutouts of comet 3I/ATLAS from August 1 and December 14, 2025. Users can switch epochs, inspect observation identifiers and coordinates, and download original FITS files, source metadata, and the official observation table. PNG previews are numerical visualizations of FITS IMAGE arrays, not AI-generated images. These comet-centered views cover different sky positions. They are not registered views of one fixed field and do not establish motion, physical change, or independent discovery. QR2 is a legacy calibration release; wavelength, WCS, PSF, masks, background and calibration need validation for scientific comparison.

Separately, a working Supabase pipeline retrieves NASA NeoWs data, archives raw responses in cloud storage, and stores dated asteroid snapshots and collection runs. An ESP32 retrieves cloud status over Wi-Fi and sends it to an Uno R3 and I2C LCD. The display showed five NEOs and zero PHA flags for the November 14 feed. PHA means potentially hazardous asteroid; classification alone does not establish impact probability.

The public demonstration dashboard brings together the real SPHEREx viewer, one archived asteroid example, and an AI-review example. It does not connect to the private database or perform live reviews. The image viewer and cloud archive currently operate separately.

The OpenAI API summarizes catalogue facts. Inputs, model and prompt versions, and human review decisions are retained. New summaries start unreviewed. The participant checked generated facts against NASA records and corrected an unsupported inference equating a non-PHA classification with no impact risk. Scheduled queue processing was verified after resolving authentication errors. A completed processing job does not mean human approval.

The historical database is central: preserving original inputs and dated snapshots enables later inspection of what a summary used, even as catalogues and models change. This prototype demonstrates preservation, not an independent trajectory or impact assessment.

Tools include TypeScript/Deno Supabase Edge Functions, PostgreSQL, cloud storage, scheduled jobs, Arduino C++, ESP32 DevKit V1, Uno R3, I2C LCD, HTML/CSS/JavaScript, GitHub Pages, Python, NumPy and Pillow. OpenAI Codex and ChatGPT assisted with ideation, research, analysis, code generation, debugging, writing, interface design, and presentation preparation. AI assistance is disclosed in the public documentation and interface. NASA observations were not AI-generated. Hardware photographs were supplied by the participant.

Future work includes linking image provenance to the database, validated matched observations, registered comparisons, and broader sky search. Satellite networks and tracking models are research concepts requiring suitable data, cooperation and validation. No satellite control, operational defense capability, impact prediction, or NASA partnership is claimed.

Dashboard: https://jpardue86.github.io/asteroid-watchers/

Code, data sample, credits and presentation: https://github.com/jpardue86/asteroid-watchers
